The Oxford History of Music notes that a Hittite slab found at Euyuk in Anatolia, dated to about 1000 BC, is carved with a bagpipe, but another reading holds that the carving shows a panpipe combined with a friction drum.
古代希臘文獻將酒囊與蘆葦管的組合與風笛相關聯。西元一世紀，狄奧·克里索斯托姆記載: Ancient Greek texts link the combination of a wine skin and reed pipes with the bagpipe. In the first century AD Dio Chrysostom records a ruler of the time (possibly the Roman emperor Nero) who could play the tibia with his mouth and blow it from a bladder held under his arm. In the second century Suetonius also describes Nero as a player of the tibia bagpipe. Modern scholarship regards such instruments as variants of the mouth-blown pipe; the bagpipe became a separate class of instrument only when the reedless pipe was added in the European Middle Ages. Early in the second millennium bagpipes begin to appear frequently in western European art and images. The Cantigas de Santa Maria, written in Galician-Portuguese in the mid-thirteenth century and compiled in Castile, depicts several types of bagpipe.

The gaida is a reed aerophone of the Balkans, in Bulgaria, a woodwind aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 422.112+422.22-62. Its parts are the blowpipe, the bag, the chanter and the drone pipe; the player blows air through the blowpipe into the bag and then presses the bag with the arm to keep a steady airflow, so that the chanter sounds continuously. The chanter is fingered with both hands, and the gaida's chanter has an additional small flea hole that helps with ornaments; the drone pipe mostly sounds a fixed harmony. The bagpipe traditionally accompanied dancing, and later also moved to the stage.
蓋達風笛由多個部分組成，其中吹嘴和音管主要採用硬木製作，常見材質包括樺木、榆木或: The gaida is made of several parts. The mouthpiece and the pipes are mainly of hardwood, commonly local durable woods such as birch, elm or juniper. The bag is usually of goatskin or sheepskin, coated inside to make it waterproof. The reed is of cane or bamboo, carefully worked to produce a particular timbre. The fittings that join the parts are mostly of wood or metal, keeping the airflow sealed and the instrument durable.
蓋達風笛音色高亢尖銳，具有穿透力強的明亮特質，帶有濃厚的民族風情。其音域主要集中: The gaida's timbre is high and sharp, bright with strong carrying power, and full of national character. Its range sits mainly in the middle and upper register, and the tone is warm but also weathered and sinewy. The instrument produces a continuous, full sound from the reed's vibration working with the constant airflow in the bag, and the resonating cavity gives it a particular penetration. Compared with the Scottish Highland bagpipe, the gaida's timbre is relatively soft and deep; compared with the clarinet its tone has more tension and thickness; compared with the saxophone it sounds more national, lacking the modern feel but gaining the flavour of history.
